title: A transform screenshot is one input body and one map: read the node, then ask what the map does to size, orientation and distance
summary: Each figure shows an input body in the History and a transform node on top. Translate, rotate and mirror preserve distances; scale, taper and free-form deformation do not, and their effect is measured by the Jacobian of the map. Because the input is often a sphere, a transform can look like a no-op, so the counts and the node name carry the evidence.

media.alt: GeoStudio window. History lists dep0: sdf_sphere and target: taper. The 3D view shows a dark oval body seen from above on a grid labelled to 7, scale bar 1 mm. The status line reads MESH 3176 verts, 6348 faces.

source.caption: GeoStudio screenshot (sandbox run): taper
source.note: Group of 13 GeoStudio screenshots of transforms applied to a single input body (7 sandbox runs, 6 toolbar runs): ffd, grow, mirror, rotate, scale, taper, translate. In the screenshots I opened the input is a sphere and no transform parameters are printed.

read_the_figure.question: What map was applied to the input body, and does the result show the change that map should cause?
read_the_figure.axes: No data axes. Left: the History with the input node (dep0) and the transform node as target. Centre: a 3D view with a labelled ground grid (labels run to about 7 for the taper view) and a scale bar (1 mm for the taper, 500 micrometres for the ffd and mirror views). Bottom: the MESH line.
look_at: The History: input row first, transform row last. The name of the transform (taper, ffd, mirror, rotate, scale, translate, grow) is the only place the operation is stated.
The outline of the result against the outline you would expect of the input. In the taper screenshot the body is seen as an oval, which is not the circle a sphere gives from above.
Where the body sits relative to the grid labels. A translate must move it, a scale must change its extent against the grid, a mirror of a centred body changes nothing visible.
The scale bar. The taper and the mirror views have different bars, so their sizes cannot be compared by eye.
The MESH line. Transforms keep the surface closed: 2V minus F should stay at 4 for a ball-like input.

If the result looks identical to the input (the ffd and mirror screenshots show a plain disc), decide whether the map is an identity, a symmetry of the input, or has parameters that are too small to see.
read_the_figure.proves: That a transform node was applied to the input and the result is still a closed body. It does not give the parameters (angle, factor, offset, lattice displacement), so it proves the kind of map but not its amount.
if_wrong: A translate or rotate screenshot whose body has not moved relative to the grid: the parameter is zero, or the sphere is centred and symmetric (a rotation of a ball about its centre changes nothing).
A mirror of a centred sphere: it looks unchanged because a ball is its own mirror image. The test needs an asymmetric input.
A scale screenshot with the same extent: the factor is one or the view auto-rescaled the grid. Compare the scale bar.
A mesh whose 2V minus F has changed from 4: the transform broke the surface (self-intersection or a fold, for example from a very strong free-form deformation).
must_check: The transform parameters are printed (angle and axis, factor, offset, lattice displacements). They are not in these windows.
The input is asymmetric, so that rotation, mirror and translation actually show.
The before state is shown next to the after state, with the same camera and scale.
A scale bar or grid that is fixed between the before and after views.
The Jacobian determinant is positive everywhere for a deformation (no fold). Not shown here.
as_drawn: Read from the status line of the screenshots I opened, exact digits.
taper (sphere input): 3176 vertices, 6348 faces, scale bar 1 mm. 2V minus F is 4, chi is 2: one closed ball-like surface.
ffd (sphere input): 1848 vertices, 3692 faces, scale bar 500 micrometres, chi is 2. The body looks like a plain disc, so either the lattice displacement is small or the view hides it.
mirror (sphere input): 4152 vertices, 8300 faces, scale bar 500 micrometres, chi is 2. A plain disc, as expected for the mirror image of a centred ball.
Not opened at full size: grow, rotate, scale, translate and the toolbar versions.

terms.meaning: Rotation plus translation. It preserves all distances and angles, so the signed distance function of the moved body is the original one evaluated at the pulled-back point.
A mirror map. It preserves distances but reverses orientation, so its determinant is minus one.
Multiplication of all coordinates by one factor s. Distances are multiplied by s and volumes by s cubed.
A scale of the cross-section that depends on height, so a cylinder becomes a cone-like body.
Embedding the body in a lattice of control points and moving the points; the space inside deforms smoothly with them.
The matrix of partial derivatives of a map. Its determinant is the local volume scale factor.
Offsetting the surface outward by a distance, which is subtracting a constant from the distance function.
Evaluating the original distance function at the inverse image of the point, which is how an implicit body is moved.

remember: A transformed implicit body is the original function evaluated at the inverse-mapped point.
Translate, rotate and mirror preserve distance; scale, taper and FFD do not.
The determinant of the Jacobian is the volume scale: 1 for translate and rotate, minus 1 for mirror, s cubed for uniform scale, s(z) squared for a taper.
A symmetric input can hide a transform: a sphere under rotation or mirroring looks unchanged.
The parameters are not in these windows, so the amount of the change is not known from the figure.

understand.title: Why a sphere is a poor test body
understand.text: The sphere is symmetric about every axis through its centre, so rotations and mirrors through the centre leave it unchanged and a small FFD is hard to see. The screenshots are still valid evidence that the node ran, but not that it did the right thing.

understand.title: What the Jacobian adds
understand.text: Where a map stretches space, distances computed in the old coordinates are wrong in the new ones. The Jacobian tells you by how much, and its determinant tells you whether the map folds space over (negative) or crushes it (zero).

steps.title: Moving an implicit body means pulling the point back
steps.note: The new body is the set of points whose preimage was inside the old one. This is the only formula needed for any transform node.

steps.title: Rotation and translation are exact
steps.note: The matrix shown rotates about the z axis. R is orthogonal, so distances are unchanged and the new function is still an exact distance.

steps.title: Mirror in a plane with unit normal n
steps.note: A reflection preserves distances but reverses orientation. Triangle winding must be flipped in the mesh or the surface will be shaded inside out.

steps.title: Uniform scale changes distance and volume
steps.note: The factor s outside keeps the function a true distance. Non-uniform scales do not have this property.

steps.title: Taper: a height-dependent scale of the cross-section
steps.note: After Barr's global deformations. The triangular matrix has determinant s squared, so a slice of thickness dz keeps its thickness but its area is multiplied by s squared.

steps.title: Free-form deformation by Bernstein polynomials
steps.note: After Sederberg and Parry. (u, v, w) are the coordinates of a point inside the lattice. With the control points on a regular grid the map is the identity, which is why an FFD with undisturbed points looks like no change.

steps.title: Grow is an offset
steps.note: Moving every surface point outward by t along the normal is subtracting t from the distance. A negative t shrinks the body.

steps.title: Counts survive rigid maps
steps.note: A rigid map or a mirror cannot change the topology of the surface. The counts in the screenshots stay at 2V minus F equal to 4 for the taper, the ffd and the mirror: 2(3176)-6348=4, 2(1848)-3692=4, 2(4152)-8300=4.

worked.title: Taper a unit circle and rotate a point
worked.problem: Illustrative values, since the window does not print parameters: a linear taper s(z) = 1 - 0.1 z. (a) By what factor does the radius of a circular cross-section at z = 2 change, and what happens to its area? (b) Where does the point (1, 0, 0) go under a rotation of 90 degrees about z?

solution.text: Radius scales by s and area by s squared (the determinant).

worked.answer: (a) The radius becomes 0.8 of its original value and the area 0.64. (b) The point goes to (0, 1, 0).

analyze.q: The taper body appears as an oval from above while a sphere appears as a circle. Is that enough to say the taper is applied about the vertical axis? What else could an oval come from?
analyze.hint: Camera angle, a non-uniform scale, or a tilt.

analyze.q: The ffd and the mirror views both show a plain disc. Give one reason each for why a correct implementation could produce that.
analyze.hint: Identity lattice or small displacement; symmetry of the input.

analyze.q: A taper has det J equal to s squared. What happens to the volume of the body as s goes to zero at the top?

evaluate.q: Are these screenshots good evidence that each transform is correct? State what you would add.
evaluate.hint: An asymmetric input, printed parameters, the before view and a Jacobian check.

evaluate.q: A scale node is shown without its factor and the grid auto-rescales. What does that do to the figure's usefulness?

create: Redesign the transform figure as a before and after pair with a fixed camera, an asymmetric input body and a caption listing the parameters.
Write a unit test that applies a random rigid map to a mesh and verifies that volume and Euler characteristic are unchanged.

checks.q: How is a body moved when it is stored as a signed distance function?
checks.hint: Which point do you evaluate the old function at?
checks.answer: By evaluating the old function at the inverse image of the point, d(phi inverse of p).

checks.q: A uniform scale by s = 2 is applied to a body of volume 3. What is the new volume?
Why does mirroring a sphere centred at the origin look like no change?
checks.hint: What symmetry does a ball have?
checks.answer: A ball is its own mirror image through its centre, so the mirrored surface is the same set of points.

checks.q: A taper screenshot shows the result but not s(z). What conclusion is safe?
checks.answer: That a taper node ran and left a closed body; nothing about how strong the taper is.

checks.q: How would you prove from a screenshot that a rotation node rotated by the stated angle?
checks.hint: Use an asymmetric input and a reference.
checks.answer: Use an asymmetric body such as a box or an L-profile, show before and after with fixed camera, and mark a vertex whose image matches R applied to its original position.
